Surname
SUR-name
n. and v.
From Old French surnom, from Latin super (over, above) and nomen (name). Webster 1828: an additional name; a name added to the baptismal or first name. In Scripture the surnaming is usually God’s act or the apostles’, and it says what a man is or will be.

Biblical Definition

Surname in Scripture is rarely a family name in the modern sense; it is an added name that declares something. God claims the act for Himself in one of the most striking verses about Cyrus, a pagan king named a century and a half before his birth: For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me (Isaiah 45:4). God names and titles a man who does not know Him, and uses him to send Israel home. The apostles surname a generous Levite from Cyprus, and the name outlasts the original: And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus (Acts 4:36). Luke uses the word plainly of a man’s second name in the message to Cornelius: call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5) — itself a surname the Lord had given him. And again of the evangelist: the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark (Acts 12:12), the young man who left Paul in Pamphylia and whom Paul later called profitable to him for the ministry.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SURNAME as an additional name; a name or appellation added to the baptismal or Christian name, and become the family name; also, an appellation added to the original name from some quality, achievement, or circumstance.

expand to see more

SURNAME, n. — An additional name; a name added to the baptismal or first name.

The family name, borne in common by the members of a household or line.

An appellation added from a quality, an achievement, or a place; as, Simon, surnamed Peter.

SURNAME, v.t. — To name or call by an appellation added to the original name.

From Latin super, over, and nomen, a name — the root also of nominate and renown.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 45:4 — "For Jacob my servant's sake, and Israel mine elect, I have even called thee by thy name: I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me."

Acts 4:36 — "And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas, (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation,) a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus,"

Acts 10:5 — "And now send men to Joppa, and call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter:"

Acts 12:12 — "And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying."

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 45 names Cyrus a century and a half before his birth, and the critical scholarship that invented a second and third Isaiah did so principally to avoid that fact.

expand to see more

The argument for dividing the book is presented as literary and historical, but its engine is the Cyrus oracle. Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 name Cyrus, call him God’s shepherd and His anointed, and describe his conquest of Babylon and his decree to rebuild the temple — and Cyrus was born some hundred and fifty years after Isaiah prophesied. If predictive prophecy of this kind is ruled out in advance, the chapters must have been written by an exilic author, and so Deutero-Isaiah was posited. The dictionary rejects the division outright and holds one prophet Isaiah. The New Testament quotes from both halves and attributes them to Isaiah by name, including John 12:38-41, which cites Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 in consecutive breaths and says These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him.

The Cyrus text also says something the church needs about God’s use of unbelieving rulers. I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me — and two verses on, I girded thee, though thou hast not known me. God titles, equips, and directs a Persian king who did not worship Him, for the sake of Jacob His servant. That is neither an endorsement of Cyrus nor a claim that he was secretly godly; it is the doctrine of providence applied to politics, and it should steady Christians who alternately baptise and despair over the rulers of their own moment. Acts 4:36 shows the gentler side of naming: the apostles called a man the son of consolation, and the church has called him that for two thousand years because it fitted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kanah (H3655), to give a title, to surname; shem (H8034), a name; Greek epikaleo (G1941), to surname, to call upon; eponomazo (G2028), to name after.

expand to see more

Hebrew kanah (H3655) — to address by an additional name, to give a title of honour; I have surnamed thee (Isaiah 45:4).

Hebrew shem (H8034) — a name; in Hebrew thought a name expresses the nature or destiny of the bearer.

Greek epikaleo (G1941) — to surname, to call by an added name; Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5).

Greek Barnabas (G921) — interpreted by Luke as son of consolation, from Aramaic bar, son, and a root of prophecy or exhortation.

Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation, exhortation; the word Luke uses to render the meaning of Barnabas.

Usage

"I have surnamed thee, though thou hast not known me (Isaiah 45:4) — a pagan king titled by God a century before his birth."

"Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas (Acts 4:36) — a name that fitted, and outlasted the original."

"Call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter (Acts 10:5) — itself a name the Lord had given."
